children: A federal appeals court on Wednesday appeared unlikely to allow President Donald Trump's administration to dismantle three small federal agencies by firing most of their employees and terminating grants.

A U.S. Department of Justice lawyer during arguments told the Boston-based 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that a lower-court judge had wrongly blocked the administration's actions affecting the Minority Business Development Agency, the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service and the U.S. Interagency Council on Homelessness.

"The upshot is that the current administration is left with the policy choices about the appropriate size and scope of three federal agencies frozen in amber, unable to change those at the president's direction," said Justice Department attorney Simon Jerome.

The agencies were all targeted by Trump in an executive order he signed in March 2025 that called for "reduction in the elements of the Federal bureaucracy that the President has determined are unnecessary."

Jerome argued that U.S. District Judge John McConnell in Rhode Island lacked jurisdiction to issue an injunction because the agencies had adopted no formal policy implementing Trump's order that could be reviewed under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Members of the three-judge panel, all appointed by Democratic presidents, expressed skepticism saying the administration's position would allow it to avoid judicial review of its efforts to dismantle agencies Congress created so long as it acted "on the down low," as U.S. Circuit Judge Seth Aframe put it.

U.S. Circuit Judge Julie Rikelman pointed to evidence presented by 21 Democratic state attorneys general who had sued over the gutting of the agencies showing they were carrying out a policy of effectively shutting themselves down. She noted two agencies eliminated all of their employees after Trump's order.
"An agency can't work without people," she said.

Rikelman, who like Aframe was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden, said that ultimately, "the challenge instead was that there was an EO that said the agencies should be closed, which is not up to the administration."

The three agencies, which are responsible for mediating labor disputes, supporting minority-owned businesses and preventing homelessness, are among seven that Trump's order had identified. The order called for them to eliminate their non-statutory components and functions to the maximum extent allowed under the law.

"The uncontested record in this case shows that defendants functionally shut down three congressionally created agencies by indiscriminately firing all or nearly all of their staff and ceasing to provide programs and services," argued New York Deputy Solicitor General Ester Murdukhayeva.

In ruling in favor of the states, McConnell had concluded that the agencies failed to offer any reasonable explanation for why they were being dismantled and that their shuttering ran afoul of the separation of powers principles enshrined in the U.S. Constitution.
The administration previously dropped its appeal concerning a fourth agency, the Institute of Museum and Library Services, but continues seeking permission to dismantle the remaining three.

The 1st Circuit had earlier declined to pause McConnell's initial preliminary injunction in the case. The three judges on that opinion included Rikelman and U.S. Circuit Judge William Kayatta, who was on the panel that heard Wednesday's appeal.
The case is State of Rhode Island v. Trump, 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, No. 26-1070.
For the states: Ester Murdukhayeva of the New York Office of the Attorney General
For the federal government: Simon Jerome of the U.S. Department of Justice
